text.headline: Rembrandt's Life Journey
text.text: An English-language overview of Rembrandt's most significant life stages, based on verifiable scholarly research.

text.headline: 1. Birth in Leiden (1606)
text.text:
Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn was baptized on July 15, 1606, in Leiden, in the Dutch Republic (modern-day Netherlands). His father, Harmen Gerritszoon van Rijn, worked as a miller, and his mother, Neeltgen Willemsdr. van Zuytbrouck, came from a family of modest means. Although some sources propose 1607 as his birth year, 1606 is most widely accepted.

Sources: Rembrandt House Museum; Bruyn, J., et al. (1982–2014). A Corpus of Rembrandt Paintings (Rembrandt Research Project).

text.headline: 2. Early Education in Leiden
text.text:
Rembrandt attended a Latin School in Leiden, demonstrating early promise. Around 1620, he briefly enrolled at Leiden University, but left to pursue painting. He likely began his formal artistic studies under Jacob van Swanenburgh in Leiden before seeking further training elsewhere.

Sources: Rembrandt Research Project; Van de Wetering, E. (2016). Rembrandt: The Complete Paintings. Taschen.

text.headline: 3. Brief Apprenticeship with Pieter Lastman in Amsterdam
text.text:
To deepen his understanding of composition and dramatic storytelling, Rembrandt spent several months under the tutelage of Pieter Lastman in Amsterdam. Lastman, known for his history paintings, influenced Rembrandt’s mastery of vivid biblical and mythological scenes.

Sources: Van de Wetering, E. (Ed.). (2005). Rembrandt: The Painter at Work. University of California Press.

text.headline: 4. Return to Leiden – First Studio
text.text:
Rembrandt returned to Leiden, where he opened a small studio, sometimes shared with fellow artist Jan Lievens. During these years, he experimented with portraiture and dramatic light effects, earning him growing local acclaim.

Sources: A Corpus of Rembrandt Paintings; Rembrandt House Museum.

text.headline: 5. Move to Amsterdam – Rise to Prominence
text.text:
Rembrandt's reputation and client base expanded rapidly, leading him to settle in Amsterdam around 1631. His collaboration with the art dealer Hendrick van Uylenburgh exposed him to influential patrons, helping him secure prestigious portrait commissions.

Sources: Schwartz, G. (1985). Rembrandt: His Life, His Work, His Time. Harry N. Abrams.

text.headline: 6. Marriage to Saskia van Uylenburgh
text.text:
On June 22, 1634, Rembrandt married Saskia van Uylenburgh, a cousin of his dealer. The union elevated Rembrandt’s social position and introduced him to higher social circles. Their relationship inspired several intimate portraits of Saskia.

Sources: Rembrandt House Museum; Van de Wetering, E. (2016). Rembrandt: The Complete Paintings. Taschen.

text.headline: 7. The House on Jodenbreestraat
text.text:
In 1639, Rembrandt purchased a grand house on Jodenbreestraat in Amsterdam (now the Rembrandt House Museum). This served as both his residence and workshop, where he trained numerous pupils and collected artworks from various masters.

Sources: Rembrandt House Museum; A Corpus of Rembrandt Paintings.

text.headline: 8. “The Night Watch” and Personal Tragedy
text.text:
In 1642, Rembrandt completed one of his most celebrated works, “The Night Watch,” demonstrating his innovative approach to group portraiture. The same year, he suffered a profound loss when Saskia passed away after prolonged illness.

Sources: Van de Wetering, E. (2013). A Corpus of Rembrandt Paintings, Vol. VI. Springer.

text.headline: 9. Decline and Bankruptcy
text.text:
A combination of reduced commissions, costly acquisitions, and personal expenses pushed Rembrandt into bankruptcy in 1656. His house, treasured art collection, and other belongings were auctioned off, forcing him to relocate to less expensive lodgings.

Sources: Schwartz, G. (1985). Rembrandt: His Life, His Work, His Time. Harry N. Abrams.

text.headline: 10. Final Years and Death in Amsterdam
text.text:
Rembrandt continued painting despite fewer commissions. He explored increasingly introspective themes, especially in biblical and portrait works. On October 4, 1669, he died in Amsterdam and was buried in an unmarked grave in the Westerkerk. Though his final years were marked by financial hardship, Rembrandt’s artistic legacy endured, influencing generations to come.

Sources: Bruyn, J., et al. (1982–2014). A Corpus of Rembrandt Paintings; Rembrandt House Museum.

text.headline: Rembrandt’s Lifetime (1606–1669)
text.text: From his birth in Leiden to his death in Amsterdam.
